description: We are *LUNARIS*, a team of passionate explorers and researchers driven by curiosity and innovation.Our project focuses on exploring Mars and identifying its environmental hazards.Using scientific data and advanced technology, we analyze dangerous zones, weather conditions, soil composition, and safe travel routes.Our mission is to make future human exploration of Mars safer, smarter, and more successful.
summary:
The Investigator is a browser-based 3D Mars exploration and route-planning tool that helps 
users compare surface traverses before a mission. It brings NASA and USGS data (Mars 
imagery, MOLA elevation, geology, rover weather and space-weather alerts) into one interactive 
globe. Users set a start and destination, or draw their own route, and the system automatically 
compares shortest, safest and lowest-oxygen routes by distance, estimated travel time, oxygen 
use, slope and a risk score, with an elevation profile and a downloadable mission report. Dust
storm and recorded hazard zones are overlaid on the map. All outputs are estimates for 
research and education, and human judgment stays final. Built by Team Lunaris.
details:
As Team Lunaris, we built The Investigator to solve a real exploration challenge: turning scattered, overwhelming Martian datasets into an intuitive, mission-ready 3D workspace. We brought together NASA and USGS digital elevation models (MOLA DEMs), rover weather telemetry, and geologic hazard maps onto an interactive globe. We wanted users to have full tactical control, so whether you define coordinate waypoints or directly draw custom traverses on the surface, our system responds instantly. To automate route planning, we engineered an A*-style search algorithm that evaluates terrain constraints and generates three distinct tactical alternatives: shortest, safest, and lowest-oxygen paths. We didn't stop at pure geometry; we modeled human survival. By coupling Tobler’s hiking function with a Minetti metabolic model scaled to Mars gravity (3.72 m/s²), we calculate real-world travel time and suit oxygen expenditure tailored to an astronaut's physiological profile.

Our goal was to eliminate the frustration of cross-referencing flat maps with hazard tables. With our tool, users can instantly assess trade-offs by comparing interactive elevation profiles, hazard overlays like active dust storms and rover entrapment sites, and comprehensive composite risk scores. Once a traverse is finalized, we generate a downloadable mission report ready for crew debriefing. We designed this to give students, educators, and mission architects a hands-on feel for how harsh Martian geography directly dictates mission survival.

To bring this to life, we developed a modern web stack using HTML5, CSS, and TypeScript/JavaScript, integrating the ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript (v4.31) to handle heavy 3D globe rendering and geospatial queries. Thinking about an astronaut's physical constraints during extravehicular activity (EVA), we implemented browser-native Web Speech APIs to enable hands-free voice commands in both English and Persian. We then deployed the whole architecture on Vercel to keep it fast and responsive from anywhere.

What makes our project creative is the synergy between hardcore physics and gamified, engaging design. Throughout development, we constantly balanced scientific fidelity with an intuitive user experience. We treated environmental risks not just as static numbers, but as dynamic constraints, all while reminding the user that while our models provide high-accuracy screening estimates, human mission judgment always remains final. We didn't just build a map—we built a cockpit for future Mars explorers.
